initial_observation.demographics: A man in his mid-80s with a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease stage 4, renal cell carcinoma (status post partial nephrectomy) and uncontrolled DM type 2 (with a recent Hb A1c 9.2%)
initial_observation.chief_complaint: generalised weakness, frequent falls, and a 1-day history of right-sided choreiform and flinging movements in his upper and lower extremity
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: He had no history of chorea and no family history of movement disorders. Family reported no unhealthy alcohol or substance use disorder. He is right-handed. His diabetic regimen at home consisted of sitagliptin 100 mg daily, though the patient reported inconsistent medication adherence over the preceding 3 months. He was also taking levothyroxine 125 µg daily, atenolol 50 mg daily and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. He had no fever, blood pressure was 141/72 mm Hg, heart rate 67, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 99% while breathing room air. Cranial nerve examination was normal, and motor strength was intact. Intermittent involuntary, non-rhythmic, flailing movements of the right arm and leg were observed. The patient was unable to execute any voluntary movements in his right arm because of hyperkinetic dyskinesia. He was alert but frustrated by these involuntary movements.
presenting_symptoms: right-sided choreiform and flinging movements in upper and lower extremity
intermittent involuntary, non-rhythmic, flailing movements of the right arm and leg

evidence_items.source_text: Laboratory tests were remarkable for acute on chronic kidney injury (serum creatinine 3.63 mg/dL, baseline 2.93 mg/dL) (normal range 0.6–1.2 mg/dL) and hyperglycaemia 597 mg/dL (normal range 70–99 mg/dL). Thyroid stimulating hormone was 2.6 (normal range 0.4–4.2 mcU/mL). Venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, serum bicarbonate was 21 mmol/L (normal range 22–29). Urinalysis showed no ketosis. Calculated serum osmolarity was 308 mosm/kg (normal 280–305 mosm/kg) making hyperosmolar hyperglycaemia state unlikely. Hb A1c level returned elevated at 17.0% (normal <6.0%).

Non-contrast CT scan of his head demonstrated a faint hyperdensity involving the left lentiform nucleus and caudate nucleus (figure 1A). Brain MRI showed an increased T1 signal intensity in the putamen on the left (figure 1B) MRI did not demonstrate evidence of acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke.

The radiological findings of basal ganglia abnormality with the sparing of internal capsule10 combined with sudden onset of hemichorea and hemiballismus along with severe hyperglycaemia led us to consider the diagnosis of DS.

The patient was admitted to the hospital for further management. Intravenous hydration and subcutaneous basal and prandial insulin were administered. Serum blood glucose levels normalised over the next 24–48 hours. Severe hemichorea-hemiballismus persisted, which impaired his ambulation and sleep. Due to severe insomnia and overnight agitation, the patient was initially treated with escalating doses of olanzapine. Low-dose clonazepam was added to the regimen on day 3 hospitalisation with minimal improvement. On day 4 olanzapine was stopped and risperidone 2 mg nightly was started with improvement in both sleep and right arm and right leg chorea-hemiballismus. The patient’s clinical symptoms of hemichorea-hemiballismus were markedly improved prior to discharge on hospital day 6.

He was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility with subcutaneous insulin, sitagliptin and risperidone with plans for ambulatory follow-up with endocrinology and neurology. The patient completed a successful course of acute rehabilitation following hospital discharge. Two months post-hospitalisation the intensity and frequency of the patient’s hemichorea involving the right upper and lower extremity had decreased and he had returned to all his usual activities. At 6-month follow-up, mild chorea in his right arm persisted.
